facts.fact_text: The first applicant is a legal entity registered under Georgian law on 8 November 2010.
With the exception of the first applicant, the remaining fourteen applicants live in Tbilisi.
The first applicant is a Georgian non-governmental organisation set up to promote and protect the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) people in Georgia.
The first applicant planned to organise a peaceful march on 17 May 2012 in the centre of Tbilisi.
The peaceful march planned by the first applicant was intended to mark the International Day Against Homophobia.
On 8 May 2012, the first applicant gave the Tbilisi City Hall prior notice of its intention to hold a peaceful demonstration on 17 May 2012.

The first applicant informed the authorities of the planned route of the march, which would start from the grounds of the Tbilisi Concert Hall and proceed to Orbeliani Square.
The first applicant informed the authorities of the approximate number of participants in the planned march.

In light of a foreseeable protest from those opposed to the LGBT community in Georgia and the general background of hostility towards sexual minorities, the first applicant specifically requested that the authorities provide sufficient protection from possible violence.

At around 1 p.m. on 17 May 2012, members of the LGBT community, staff members of Identoba and other LGBT activists, including the second to fourteenth applicants, gathered at the Tbilisi Concert Hall area, totalling approximately thirty people.
Shortly before the beginning of the demonstration on 17 May 2012, members of the Orthodox Parents' Union arrived in the Tbilisi Concert Hall area.
Shortly before the beginning of the demonstration on 17 May 2012, members of the Saint King Vakhtang Gorgasali's Brotherhood arrived in the Tbilisi Concert Hall area.
Journalists were present at the Tbilisi Concert Hall area shortly before the demonstration on 17 May 2012, recording interviews with the LGBT marchers.
Approximately 200 metres from the starting point of the march on 17 May 2012, members of the Orthodox Parents' Union and the Saint King Vakhtang Gorgasali's Brotherhood confronted the LGBT marchers.
When the LGBT marchers reached Rustaveli Avenue on 17 May 2012, they were met by a hundred or more counter-demonstrators who were particularly aggressive and verbally offensive.
The counter-demonstrators blocked the LGBT marchers' way on Rustaveli Avenue by making a human chain and encircling the marchers, making it impossible for them to pass.
The LGBT marchers were subjected to threats of physical assault and to insults by the counter-demonstrators on Rustaveli Avenue on 17 May 2012.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 was adopted by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe on 31 March 2010 on measures to combat discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 provides that member states should ensure effective, prompt and impartial investigations into alleged cases of crimes and other incidents where the sexual orientation or gender identity of the victim is reasonably suspected to have constituted a motive for the perpetrator.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 provides that member states should ensure that particular attention is paid to the investigation of crimes and incidents allegedly committed by law enforcement officials or by other persons acting in an official capacity, and that those responsible are effectively brought to justice and, where appropriate, punished in order to avoid impunity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 provides that member states should ensure that when determining sanctions, a bias motive related to sexual orientation or gender identity may be taken into account as an aggravating circumstance.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 provides that member states should take appropriate measures to ensure that the right to freedom of expression can be effectively enjoyed without discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, in accordance with Article 10 of the Convention.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 provides that member states should take appropriate measures at national, regional and local levels to ensure that the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, as enshrined in Article 11 of the Convention, can be effectively enjoyed without discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 provides that member states should ensure that law enforcement authorities take appropriate measures to protect participants in peaceful demonstrations in favour of the human rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons from any attempts to unlawfully disrupt or inhibit the effective enjoyment of their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 provides that public authorities at all levels should be encouraged to publicly condemn, notably in the media, any unlawful interferences with the right of individuals and groups of individuals to exercise their freedom of expression and peaceful assembly, notably when related to the human rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons.

The Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 12 September 2014 noted that the numbers of bias-motivated attacks against LGBTI persons cited are most certainly lower than the actual occurrence, due to the reluctance of victims to report violence to police, inter alia because of fears that their sexual orientation would be disclosed to family members.

The Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 12 September 2014 noted that NGOs had expressed serious concerns regarding the lack of effective investigation and adequate punishment for perpetrators of attacks against LGBTI persons in Georgia.

The Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 12 September 2014 encouraged increased efforts to enhance tolerance and non-discrimination among the majority population in Georgia, and emphasised the importance for authorities, public actors and community leaders to send an unambiguous message in favour of human rights and tolerance, and against violence, hate speech and discrimination.

The Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 12 September 2014 welcomed the plans to develop comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation in Georgia and strongly encouraged the establishment of an equality body with the power to sanction instances of discrimination, including on actors from the private sector.

The Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 12 September 2014 stated that hate crimes should be effectively investigated and qualified as such by law enforcement bodies in Georgia, that the bias motive should be taken into account as an aggravating circumstance as already provided for by national legislation, and that perpetrators should receive punishment commensurate to the gravity of the offence.

In its 2013 Annual Review of the situation of the LGBT community in Georgia, the International Lesbian and Gay Association (ILGA) noted that in March 2012 an amendment to Article 53 of the Criminal Code of Georgia was adopted to tackle intolerance on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, making homophobic or transphobic motivation an aggravating factor in sentencing perpetrators of crimes.

The International Lesbian and Gay Association (ILGA) noted in its 2013 Annual Review that the legislative change to Article 53 of the Criminal Code of Georgia was adopted as a response to recommendations from the European Commission against Racism and Intolerance.

The International Lesbian and Gay Association (ILGA) noted in its 2013 Annual Review that the government of Georgia did not take measures to ensure effective implementation of the amended Article 53 of the Criminal Code, such as training the relevant police officers or taking actions to build confidence between law enforcement forces and the LGBT community.

The International Lesbian and Gay Association (ILGA) collected information on seven hate crimes perpetrated against LGBT persons in Georgia during 2013, including various types of attacks such as rape, and various types of physical violence threats including death threats.

Some of the hate crimes collected by the International Lesbian and Gay Association (ILGA) in its 2013 Annual Review targeted the organisers and participants of the International Day Against Homophobia (IDAHO) demonstration that took place in May 2012 in Georgia.
